prime.problem: Once a queue forms, the order you read it in is the latency. FCFS makes every short chat wait behind every long job; SJF fixes that and starves the long jobs; priority protects one class and can starve the other. Pick a policy without knowing what it costs and someone ends up waiting 37 seconds.
prime.fits: Sixth card of group 3. step() admits "in policy order" through WaitQueue.peek(); this card fills in that order: the data structure, the sort key, and what each choice does to TTFT and to the worst case.
expect: FCFS, SJF/SRPT, priority, VTC fair share, aging, EDF, MLFQ, LPM
each as a data structure plus a sort key
E5: SJF ≈ 77× better median, worst case 22.4 → 37.3 s
linear aging as a fixed heap key
prime.goal: Choose a policy for a given workload, state its container and cost, predict whom it helps and whom it starves with numbers, and explain why policy changes who waits but not how much gets done.

attend: At 20 req/s FCFS and SJF give the same TTFT. What has to be true before a policy decides anything?
Why does a 100%-noise length predictor keep almost all of SJF's gain?
Why can linear aging stay a fixed heap key, while HRRN forces SGLang to re-sort every pass?
Under fairness, tenant B's share rises to 21% though it sends 10% of requests. What does that tell you?
Why can no α in the aging sweep give both the 97 ms median and the 22 s worst case?

must: The policy is only the order step() reads the waiting queue → the same work gets done (6,451–6,584 tok/s in every run) → it decides who waits, and only once requests arrive faster than they finish

SJF admits short jobs first → the median wait collapses (7,490 → 97.2 ms at 55 req/s) → long jobs lose every tie → worst E2E 22.4 → 37.3 s → pair it with aging, and a rough predictor is enough because it only has to rank short vs long
Priority classes put interactive first (36.1 ms p50) → batch waits longer (9,760 ms) → if the high class alone fills the GPU, batch starves → add aging or a reserved share

VTC keeps a weighted service counter per tenant and serves the least-served → a burst from one tenant stops costing the others (B: 8,353 → 46 ms) → the heavy tenant pays a little (A: 9,279 → 10,974 ms)
elevated: Every waiting request ages at the same rate → size − α·(now − arrival) orders like size + α·arrival → linear aging is a fixed O(log W) heap key, while ratio keys (HRRN) reorder over time
reference: the published multiples (FastServe 31.4×, Andes 4.7×, Learning to Rank 2.8×)
SGLang's policy names and the 128-waiting FCFS fallback
the WaitQueue code details (_seq tie-break, _n counter)

compress.prompt: From memory, write each of FCFS, SJF, priority and fair as "container · key · push/pick cost · who it starves". Then write one sentence on why none of them changes throughput, and one on what to do when every order fails.
checklist: FCFS: deque · arrival · O(1)/O(1) · nobody, but head-of-line blocking
SJF: heap · prompt + predicted · O(log W) · long jobs
priority: heap or K deques · (class, arrival) · low class
fair: per-tenant deques + counters · least served · O(T) · the heavy tenant pays a little
policy changes who waits, not tokens/s; under sustained overload, shed load or add replicas

retrieve.q: Explain why SJF cuts median TTFT about 77× at 55 req/s but does nothing at 20 req/s.
answer: at 20 req/s a request is admitted the step after it arrives: there is no queue to reorder
at 55 req/s the queue keeps growing, so order decides who waits
SJF lets the many short requests skip ahead of the few long ones

retrieve.q: Walk through how the fair WaitQueue picks the next request when tenant A has been served 9,120 weighted tokens and tenant B 912, and what happens when a new tenant C appears.
answer: pick the backlogged tenant with the smallest counter: B
pop B's oldest request; charge prompt tokens + 2 × output tokens as it runs
C starts at the lowest active counter, so it can't bank credit it didn't use

retrieve.q: Interactive and batch traffic share the GPUs. Compare strict priority with priority + aging, and say what each risks.
answer: strict priority: interactive TTFT p50 36.1 ms, but batch is never admitted if interactive alone fills the GPU
priority + aging: batch eventually rises, capping its wait
cost: aging gives back some of the interactive gain and adds a knob (α)

compare.q: Admission control and policy both decide who waits. What does each control that the other can't, and which one fixes sustained overload?
answer: policy reorders requests already in the queue
admission control decides whether a request enters at all (429, early rejection)
under sustained overload every order just picks who suffers; only admission control or more capacity fixes it

compare.q: Cache-aware LPM is a policy whose key depends on what is cached now. How is that different from SJF's key, and what does it cost?
answer: SJF's key is fixed per request, so a heap works
LPM's key changes as the cache changes, so the queue must be re-sorted and prefix-matched each pass (O(W log W))
SGLang falls back to FCFS above 128 waiting to cap that cost; cold-prefix requests can wait behind warm ones

predict.q: Traffic is bursty: 70 req/s for 10 s, then 10 req/s for 20 s, repeating. Before simulating: does SJF still starve long jobs as badly as in E5's sustained 55 req/s?
predict.answer: Much less. In the quiet periods the queue drains, so every long job eventually gets admitted; SJF only delays it through the burst. Starvation in E5 comes from the queue never emptying. The card makes the same point about aging: with bursts that drain between peaks the trade is kinder.

apply.task: Four requests wait: A (arrived 0.0 s, size 5,000 tokens), B (1.0 s, 700), C (2.0 s, 1,200), D (2.5 s, 300), where size = prompt + predicted output. Write the admission order under FCFS, SJF, and linear aging with key size + α·arrival for α = 1,000 and α = 3,000 tokens per second. Then say which α protects A, and at what cost to D.
apply.done: FCFS: A, B, C, D. SJF: D (300), B (700), C (1,200), A (5,000). α = 1,000: keys A 5,000, B 1,700, C 3,200, D 2,800 → B, D, C, A. α = 3,000: A 5,000, B 3,700, C 7,200, D 7,800 → B, A, C, D. The larger α moves A from last to second and pushes D, the shortest, to last.
apply.hint: A smaller key goes first; arrival time in seconds times α is the "size" forgiven.
